pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 5–7; rainforests hold an enormous variety of plants — towering kapok and Brazil nut trees, climbing vines called lianas, colourful orchids that grow on tree branches, giant water lilies, and huge leaves that funnel rainwater.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS1 Y1 'Plants' (identify and name common/wild plants; parts of plants) and Y2 'Living things and their habitats'.
• Standards—US: NGSS 2-LS4-1 (diversity of life in habitats); 1-LS1-1 (external parts of plants/animals); K-ESS3-1.
• Operational details: showcase the VARIETY and the giant scale — trees taller than houses, vines that climb, flowers that grow high up on branches instead of the ground, and leaves so big they channel rain. Give each plant a hook (kapok = giant tree; liana = climbing rope; orchid = flower that lives on a branch; giant lily = big enough to sit a child; drip-leaf = funnels rain). Seed the idea that plants have clever shapes for a wet, crowded, shady world (developed fully in the 7–9 adaptations topic).
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5) name two rainforest plants; Tier B (6) describe one (a giant tree, a climbing vine, a flower on a branch); Tier C (7) explain that rainforest plants come in a huge variety and have special shapes for the wet, crowded forest.
bestPractices: Emphasise scale and variety with comparisons children feel (trees taller than a house, a lily big enough to sit on)
Give each plant one vivid hook so the variety is memorable, not a blur
Introduce the surprising idea that some plants (orchids) grow high on branches, not in the ground — a hook for epiphytes later
Point out clever shapes (climbing vines, rain-funnelling leaves) to seed plant adaptations
Use real photographs to convey the lushness and unfamiliar forms
keyRepresentations: Plant gallery cards: kapok, Brazil nut tree, liana, orchid, giant water lily, drip-tip leaf
Scale comparison (giant tree vs house; giant lily vs child)
Branch close-up showing an orchid growing ON a tree, not in soil
Rain funnelling off a huge pointed leaf
commonMisconceptions: All rainforest plants are ordinary and small — many are giants or grow in surprising ways
Flowers only grow in the ground — orchids grow high up on tree branches
Vines are separate stringy things — lianas are climbing plants using trees to reach the light
Big leaves are just decoration — their shape helps shed heavy rain
Plants are the same everywhere — rainforests have an extraordinary variety of plant forms

learn.summary: For ages 5–7: rainforests hold an enormous variety of plants — towering kapok and Brazil nut trees, climbing vines called lianas, colourful orchids (many of which grow high on tree branches rather than in the ground), giant water lilies big enough to hold a small child, and huge pointed leaves that funnel rainwater off their tips. The core goal is recognising this variety and giant scale with vivid hooks, plus seeding the surprising idea that some plants grow high up and have clever shapes for a wet, crowded, shady world (adaptations are developed fully in a later 7–9 topic).

activities.title: Rainforest plant gallery: variety and giant scale
feedback: If a child thinks all rainforest plants are small and ordinary, show the scale comparison (giant tree vs house; lily vs child) and name the giants.
If a child says flowers only grow in the ground, return to the branch close-up: the orchid perches high on a tree branch, not in soil.
If a child thinks the vine is just a rope or part of the tree, point out the liana is its own plant, rooted in the ground, that climbs the tree to reach the light above the shady floor.
If a child says the big leaf is just decoration, show the rain funnelling off its pointed tip and connect shape to shedding heavy rain.
If a child assumes plants look the same everywhere, place several of the rainforest plants side by side so they feel how many different forms live in one forest.
Praise a correct name plus one described feature (e.g. 'the orchid is a flower that grows on a branch') rather than just naming.
activities.rationale: At 5–7 the objective is recognising plant variety and scale, which is well served by browsing a rich set of real images with per-plant hooks; concrete scale references and a branch close-up make the 'variety and surprising forms' idea memorable rather than a blur. An interactive gallery where tapping each plant reveals its name, scale hook, and clever form may support self-paced exploration, but a printed photo set with spoken hooks works too; the relative efficacy of these formats is not established by the source row.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils identify and name common and wild plants and describe basic plant parts, and study living things in habitats
Students observe the diversity of life in habitats
Rainforests contain enormous plant variety including emergent kapok and Brazil nut trees, climbing lianas, epiphytic orchids growing on branches, giant water lilies, and large drip-tip leaves
learnerActions: Look at real photographs of a kapok tree, Brazil nut tree, liana, orchid, giant water lily, and a drip-tip leaf.
For the kapok, compare it to a scale reference such as a child-sized figure or a house to feel 'taller than a house'.
For the liana, trace how the rope-like vine spirals up a trunk toward the light.
For the orchid, look at a branch close-up showing the flower growing ON the tree, not in soil.
For the giant water lily, see a pad big enough to hold a small child floating on water.
For the drip-tip leaf, watch or imagine a stream of rain tipping neatly off the pointed tip.
Give each plant a one-line hook and say it aloud: kapok = giant tree; liana = climbing rope; orchid = flower that lives on a branch; giant lily = big enough to sit a child; drip-leaf = funnels rain.
Name at least two rainforest plants, then describe one of them (a giant tree, a climbing vine, or a flower on a branch).
activities.intendedInsight: Rainforest plants aren't all ordinary and small — they come in an extraordinary variety, many are giants, and some grow in surprising places and shapes for a wet, crowded, shady forest.

activities.title: Why such strange shapes? A hook for clever forms
feedback: If a child can't say why a plant climbs or grows tall, connect height and climbing to reaching sunlight above the dark, shady forest floor.
If a child thinks the orchid high on a branch must be stealing from the tree, explain it only perches up high to reach light and makes its own food — it doesn't feed on the tree.
Encourage the child to link one shape to one job (pointed leaf → sheds rain; vine → climbs to light).
activities.rationale: A short physical or interactive micro-action (pouring rain off a leaf, miming a vine climbing to light) is a proposed way to make a plant behaviour felt and may plant an early, age-appropriate seed for adaptations, while the main variety-recognition goal stays with the gallery. This is an enrichment hook, not a full adaptations lesson, and its effectiveness relative to the gallery is untested.
learnerActions: Act out or pour water onto a large pointed leaf (a real leaf, or a laminated or waxed card stand-in that only approximates the real leaf — plain paper soaks up water and may not shed it) and watch it run off the tip; describe where the rain goes.
Pretend to be a liana: start low in the 'shade' and climb (with hands or a rope) up toward a 'light' at the top of the forest.
Open a lift-the-flap or answer the question 'Why such strange shapes?' and talk about the wet, crowded, shady forest.
Point to one plant and say one clever thing about its shape (a vine that climbs to reach light, a leaf that funnels rain).
activities.intendedInsight: Some rainforest plants have clever shapes and habits — climbing to reach light, funnelling off heavy rain — that help them thrive in a giant green world. This seeds the later idea of plant adaptations.

activities.title: Check and discuss: the orchid on the branch
feedback: If the child says 'yes, it takes food from the tree', gently correct: the orchid only perches for light and makes its own food; it doesn't feed on the tree.
If the child can't give a reason for growing high, link it to reaching sunlight above the dark floor.

A full answer names several plants, explains the orchid perches only to reach light and makes its own food, and links tall/climbing growth to competing for sunlight. A partial answer knows some plants and that they grow tall but still thinks the orchid feeds off the tree or can't say why it's high up.
Reward reasons, not just yes/no: the 'why' is what shows real understanding.
activities.rationale: A reason-giving prompt helps distinguish a child who holds 'epiphytes are parasites' from one who understands perching-for-light, because it asks for the light-not-theft reason rather than a yes/no guess. Matching tasks check recall of the named plants after the gallery has built recognition.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils identify and name common and wild plants and describe basic plant parts, and study living things in habitats
learnerActions: Respond to: 'An orchid grows high up on the branch of a big rainforest tree, not in the ground. Is the orchid stealing food from the tree like a thief? Say yes or no, and then say WHY it grows up there.'
Match each plant to a feature (giant tree, climbing vine, flower on a branch, rain-funnelling leaf) after browsing the gallery.

Discuss follow-ups: Where does a plant get its food — the soil, or something else? Why would it be hard for a small plant to live on the dark forest floor? What is a liana, and how does it reach the top of the forest?
activities.intendedInsight: A perching orchid isn't a thief: it grows high only to reach sunlight and makes its own food from sunlight, taking water from air and rain — not from the tree. Tall and climbing growth is about competing for light above the shady floor.

constraints: Core objective at this age is recognising plant variety and giant scale; the 'clever shapes/adaptations' material is a seed and hook, developed fully in a later 7–9 adaptations topic — don't over-teach mechanism here.
A matching or name-the-plant check confirms recall of plant names but does not by itself elicit the child's own reasoning; use the 'why does it grow up there' prompt to surface understanding.

Interactive tapping, lift-the-flaps, live rain-off-the-leaf and grow-a-vine micro-interactions are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — they are illustrative, not required; a photo set with spoken hooks and a paper leaf can meet the same goals.
Paper or card leaf and plant cutouts are thin approximations with slight thickness; use them to represent the real plants, not as exact models, and say so where they are used.
Keep scale comparisons concrete (taller than a house, big enough to sit a child) rather than vague 'very big'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; all sources[].claim entries remain marked verified:false in the source row and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Activity 2 ('Why such strange shapes?') carries sourceClaims:[] because no source claim directly supports its teaching principle (that a micro-action makes behaviour felt / seeds adaptations); the sources establish plant variety and curriculum coverage of the topic only.

Activity 3's retained KS1 naming claim supports only its matching-recall subtask; no source claim directly supports its core epiphyte-reasoning principle, which is retained as seed/discussion material for this age rather than a required mastery target.

The source states orchids 'make their own food from sunlight and take water from the air and rain, not from the tree.' Botanically, epiphytic orchids are non-parasitic and photosynthesise, so the core teaching point (not a parasite; perches for light) is sound; the simplified phrasing is acceptable for ages 5–7 but omits nuance (some nutrients from debris/air), which does not affect the misconception being corrected.

The assessment's probeDeeper and correctAnswer push into epiphyte/light-competition ideas that the pedagogy marks as belonging to the later 7–9 adaptations topic; retained here as discussion/seed material, not as a required mastery target for 5–7.
'Compete for sunlight' as the reason plants grow tall is a reasonable simplification; presented as a hook rather than a complete explanation.

Of the five source commonMisconceptions, four receive dedicated activity 1 feedback and the fifth ('plants are the same everywhere') is now addressed by a dedicated feedback item plus the overall variety theme.

probeDeeper: Where does a plant get its food from — the soil, or something else?
Why would it be hard for a small plant to live down on the dark forest floor?
What is a liana, and how does it reach the top of the forest?
assess.correctAnswer: No — the orchid isn't stealing from the tree. It just perches on the branch to get up high near the sunlight, because plants on the dark floor can't get enough light. It makes its own food from sunlight and takes water from the air and rain, not from the tree. Climbing up is how it reaches the light.

errorPatterns.pattern: epiphytes are parasites — 'the orchid steals food or water from the tree'
errorPatterns.nextMove: epiphytes only perch for light and make their own food; they don't feed on the tree
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — it takes its food from the tree it sits on
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the perching plant takes food from the tree

errorPatterns.pattern: plants grow tall for no reason — misses competing for light
errorPatterns.nextMove: link height and climbing to reaching sunlight above the shady floor
errorPatterns.revealedBy: can't say why rainforest plants grow so tall or climb

responseLevels.gap: Says perching plants steal from the tree; no sense of plants competing for light.
responseLevels.full: Names several rainforest plants, explains epiphytes perch only to reach light and make their own food (not parasites), and links tall/climbing growth to competing for sunlight.
responseLevels.partial: Knows some rainforest plants and that they grow tall, but still thinks epiphytes feed off the tree or can't say why they're high up.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: An orchid grows high up on the branch of a big rainforest tree, not in the ground. Is the orchid stealing food from the tree like a thief? Tell me yes or no, and then tell me WHY it grows up there.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding 'epiphytes are parasites' says the orchid steals food; the concept child explains it only perches for light and makes its own food. The reason-tier forces the light-not-theft reason.
